name: Electron Beam Ion Source (EBIS)
description: EBIS strips electrons from atoms using an intense electron beam trapped in a strong solenoid field, creating highly charged ions of nearly any element from helium to uranium. It replaced the older Tandem Van de Graaff in 2011 and delivers short, intense ion pulses to the Booster.

name: Polarized Ion Source (OPPIS)
description: The Optically Pumped Polarized Ion Source makes proton beams whose spins are aligned in a chosen direction. These polarized protons let RHIC study the origin of proton spin, which no other collider can do.

name: Linear Accelerator (Linac)
description: The 200 MeV linear accelerator uses a chain of Alvarez drift-tube cavities to boost protons from the polarized ion source before injecting them into the Booster synchrotron.

name: Booster Synchrotron
function: Boosts ions and protons before the AGS
description: The Booster is a compact circular accelerator that takes beams from the Linac or EBIS and raises their energy so they can be injected efficiently into the Alternating Gradient Synchrotron. It also supplies beams to the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory.

name: Alternating Gradient Synchrotron (AGS)
function: Accelerates beams to RHIC injection energy
description: The AGS, a Nobel-winning machine that has run since 1960, uses alternating-gradient focusing to accelerate protons and ions to the energy RHIC needs. It also bunches the beam and sends it down the AGS-to-RHIC transfer line.

name: AGS-to-RHIC Transfer Line
function: Carries beam from the AGS into the RHIC rings
description: A beamline of bending and focusing magnets that moves bunches from the AGS and splits them into RHIC's two rings, the Blue ring and the Yellow ring.

name: NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL)
function: Simulates cosmic radiation for space research
description: NSRL uses beams from the Booster to reproduce the heavy-ion radiation astronauts face in space. It is used to study radiation damage to cells, tissue and electronics.

name: Blue Ring Superconducting Dipoles
function: Bends the clockwise beam around the ring
description: The Blue ring carries beam clockwise. Its superconducting niobium-titanium dipole magnets, cooled to about 4 K with liquid helium, produce fields of roughly 3.5 tesla that bend the beam around the 3.8 km circumference.

name: Yellow Ring Superconducting Dipoles
function: Bends the counter-clockwise beam around the ring
description: The Yellow ring carries beam counter-clockwise, in the opposite direction to the Blue ring. The two independent rings let RHIC collide different species, such as gold on gold or polarized protons on protons, at six crossing points.

name: Quadrupole Focusing Magnets
description: Superconducting quadrupole magnets sit between the dipoles and work like lenses, squeezing the beam so that it stays narrow and stable over billions of turns. Stronger quadrupoles near the experiments focus the beam to a tiny spot for collisions.

name: RF Cavities
description: Radio-frequency cavities give the particles their energy boost each turn and hold them in tight bunches. RHIC uses 28 MHz cavities for acceleration and 197 MHz storage cavities to keep bunches short during collisions.

name: Interaction Point
function: Where the two beams cross and collide
description: At each of the six interaction regions the Blue and Yellow beams are steered into each other. Collisions of gold ions briefly recreate the quark-gluon plasma, the hot dense matter that filled the universe microseconds after the Big Bang.

name: STAR Detector
description: The Solenoidal Tracker At RHIC uses a large solenoid magnet and a time projection chamber to record thousands of charged particles produced in each heavy-ion collision. It is the main detector studying quark-gluon plasma and proton spin.

name: sPHENIX Detector
description: sPHENIX is a calorimeter-based detector built around a superconducting solenoid. It measures jets and upsilon particles to probe how quark-gluon plasma behaves at different length scales. It succeeded the original PHENIX detector.

name: Beam Position Monitor
description: Pickup electrodes inside the beam pipe sense the electric field of passing bunches and report the beam's position. Operators use the readings to keep the beam centered and to correct its orbit.

name: Vacuum Pump
function: Keeps the beam pipe at ultra-high vacuum
description: Beam pipes must be nearly empty of gas, or the particles would scatter off molecules and be lost. Ion and cryogenic pumps maintain an ultra-high vacuum along the whole ring.

name: Magnet Cross-Section (Cutaway)
function: Shows how a cryogenic magnet is built
description: The cutaway reveals the layers of an RHIC magnet: the beam pipe, the superconducting coils, a steel yoke, a thermal shield and the outer vacuum vessel. The layers keep the coils cold and the beam pipe evacuated.

name: Cryogenic Valve Box
function: Controls liquid helium flow to the magnets
description: Valve boxes distribute liquid helium from the refrigerator to each sector of the ring and route it back as cold gas. Keeping the magnets near 4 K lets the superconducting coils carry current with no resistance.

name: Quench Protection and Service Cabinet
description: If a superconducting magnet warms up and loses superconductivity, a quench, its stored energy must be removed quickly. These cabinets detect quenches and safely dump the energy, protecting the magnets.

name: Access Shaft
description: Access shafts placed around the ring let crews and equipment reach the underground tunnel for maintenance and installation.

name: Utility Gantry
description: The gantry is a truss structure holding cable trays, cryogenic and water piping, and the large DC cables that power the magnets.
